question: A researcher studying whether smoking causes bladder cancer selects 200 bladder cancer patients and 200 cancer-free controls, then interviews all about their past smoking history. The appropriate measure of association for this design is:

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: RR requires knowing the incidence in exposed and unexposed groups. Because this case-control design starts from disease status (not exposure), true incidence cannot be directly calculated.
Correct. Case-control studies calculate the OR — the ratio of odds of exposure among cases to odds of exposure among controls. When disease is rare, OR approximates RR.
AR (risk difference) requires incidence data from cohort or experimental studies — not obtainable directly from a case-control design.
Prevalence ratio comes from cross-sectional studies. This is a case-control study, which yields an Odds Ratio.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall: Case-control studies work backwards from disease status, so incidence (needed for RR) is unknown. The OR is the correct measure here. OR ≈ RR only when disease prevalence is low.
Well done. Case-control → OR; Cohort → RR. When the disease is rare (< 10%), OR closely approximates RR — a key Park teaching point.
